157e36de08:
This chapter is about what happens to state once an agent runs for more than a handful of turns. It covers three things:

  • where the agent remembers things: the window, a facts block, the memory tool, stores, checkpoints;
  • how it keeps its own context from filling up: trimming, clearing tool results, compaction, notes, sub-agent isolation;
  • how LangGraph, Strands Agents and PydanticAI package the same tool-use loop in three different shapes.

The story runs from cognitive-architecture memory models and MemGPT through Anthropic's memory tool and server-side context editing. Implementations are in Python, with Java/Spring equivalents.
1c7e823605: Reading time: 2.5 to 3 hours  ·  Companion code, 16 runnable examples: ccdvf-companion/03-agent-patterns/ (run bash run_all.sh). Everything works offline with a fake client. The three frameworks are replaced by small stubs that copy their public shape, so nothing needs to be installed.
f07cb50a41:
Boundaries with other chapters. Chapter 01 decides workflow versus agent, and covers the five workflow patterns and hierarchies. Chapter 02 builds the loop, the Claude Agent SDK harness and hooks. Chapter 16 treats context engineering as a full discipline (system prompt design, retrieval, attention budget).

This chapter assumes the loop from chapter 02. It focuses on what the loop does with memory and context over a long run, and on the three third-party frameworks the objective names.
dfea95b28a:
An agent's only working state is the message list your harness sends on every call, so every memory or context technique is a policy about what goes into that list, what is taken out of it, and what is kept somewhere else and loaded back by a tool.

Frameworks such as LangGraph, Strands Agents and PydanticAI run the same send, check stop_reason, run tools, append loop; they differ in who owns the control flow (you, through a graph, or the model) and in what they make durable (checkpoints) or guaranteed (typed, validated output).
68e806e272:
Everything else in this chapter follows from those two sentences.

  • "Short-term memory" is the list itself.
  • "Long-term memory" is storage outside the list. It only matters when a tool or the harness reads it back in.
  • "Context-window management" is a set of edits you make to the list (or ask the API to make), so that it stays small, valid and focused.
  • A "sub-agent" is a second list, used for a sub-task and then thrown away.
  • A "checkpoint" is the list (plus any other state) written to disk after each step, so a crashed or paused run can continue.
  • A "framework" is someone else's implementation of the loop and those policies, with opinions about what you should configure.
a3267bf1fc:
Sub-objective 1.3 is worth 4.9% of the CCDV-F exam: about two or three questions out of 53. They're scenario questions. An agent forgets a customer preference between sessions. A long investigation starts repeating itself. A run needs to pause for a supervisor's approval. A team needs typed output. A team on AWS wants minimal orchestration code.

Your job is to name the mechanism that fixes the cause. The table below maps exam phrasing to the section of this chapter that teaches the answer.
e18a62335e:
A note on vocabulary. The exam outline says "memory types (short-term, long-term, memory tool)". Different sources slice memory differently: working, episodic, semantic, procedural; or in-context versus external; or thread-scoped versus cross-thread.

Section 05 gives a taxonomy organised by lifetime. Lifetime decides where the memory must live and how it gets back into the window. And it maps cleanly onto the three words the outline uses.
91a7fa2314: None of the memory and context patterns in agent frameworks is new. Each one solves a problem that cognitive scientists, database engineers or early LLM builders ran into first. Know the lineage and the exam's preferences become predictable. Keep the working set small. Store durable facts outside it. Make state explicit enough to inspect and resume.
5940a0682e:
George Miller's 1956 paper "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two" argued that human short-term memory holds only a handful of items. Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968) proposed the modal model: sensory input, a small short-term store, and a large long-term store, with rehearsal moving items between them.

Baddeley and Hitch (1974) refined short-term memory into "working memory", a workspace with limited capacity where reasoning actually happens. Endel Tulving (1972) split long-term memory into episodic (what happened, when) and semantic (facts). Later work added procedural memory (how to do things).
702fc1434f:
The parallel with a language model is close enough to be useful, and loose enough to be dangerous. The context window is a working memory. Everything the model reasons over must be in it, and it has a fixed capacity. Weights are a kind of semantic and procedural memory, but frozen at training time.

What the model lacks is any mechanism to move items from working memory into a durable store and back. Agent memory designs are, in effect, an external hippocampus built by the harness.
c15a6c9c60:
Soar (Laird, Newell, Rosenbloom, 1987) and ACT-R (Anderson, 1990s) were complete "cognitive architectures". These programs had an explicit working memory, a long-term declarative store, and production rules. A decision cycle read working memory, chose an action, and wrote results back. Soar later added explicit episodic and semantic memory modules.

These systems are the ancestors of the "agent loop plus memory store" picture. Their lesson for us is architectural: memory is a set of separate stores with different access paths, not one bigger buffer.
49d79b150f:
The transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) made the context window the unit of "attention". Every token can attend to every other token in the window, and to nothing outside it. Windows grew from 512 tokens to 2k, 8k, 100k and beyond. But they stayed finite, cost grew with length, and quality on long inputs proved uneven.

Retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020) took the database approach. Keep knowledge in an external index, and pull the relevant pieces into the prompt at query time. RAG is long-term memory for documents. Agent memory reuses the same retrieval machinery for experience.
54cea6c5dd:
Three 2023 papers framed modern agent memory.

  • Generative Agents (Park et al.) gave simulated characters a "memory stream" of observations. A retrieval function scored recency, importance and relevance. Periodic "reflection" summarised memories into higher-level ones.
  • MemGPT (Packer et al.) treated the context window like RAM in an operating system. It had a small main context, an external archive, and functions the model calls to page information in and out. The system warned the model when memory pressure rose.
  • Reflexion (Shinn et al.) stored the agent's own verbal self-critique between attempts.

At the same time, LangChain shipped "memory" classes (buffer, window, summary, summary-buffer). They're the direct ancestors of today's sliding-window and summarising conversation managers.
6ec142581b: MemGPT in particular is worth remembering. Anthropic's memory tool follows its central idea: let the model decide what to save and look up, through tool calls. But it drops the OS metaphor in favour of plain files.
1feeee7da5:
LangChain's team released LangGraph (early 2024) after users found linear chains and opaque agent executors hard to control. LangGraph modelled an application as a state machine with explicit nodes, edges and a typed state object. It added checkpointers that persist state after each step under a thread id. They enable resume, time travel and human-in-the-loop interrupts.

The Pydantic team released PydanticAI (late 2024), bringing type-checked dependencies and validated outputs to agents.

In December 2024 Anthropic published "Building effective agents". It distinguished workflows from agents and catalogued the workflow patterns (chapter 01). It advised starting with direct API calls, and adding framework layers only when they earn their place.
47724c90c0:
In May 2025 AWS open-sourced Strands Agents, a model-driven SDK. You supply a model, a system prompt and tools, and the model runs the loop. It ships conversation managers (sliding window, summarising) and session persistence.

In September 2025 Anthropic added two API features aimed squarely at long-running agents:

  • context editing, which clears old tool results server-side when the prompt crosses a threshold;
  • the memory tool, a client-executed file interface under /memories that lets Claude store and retrieve information across conversations.

Anthropic's "Effective context engineering for AI agents" post the same month named the discipline. Treat context as a finite attention budget. Prefer just-in-time retrieval. Use compaction, structured note-taking and sub-agent architectures for long horizons.

Server-side compaction followed (a compact_20260112 context-management edit at the time of writing). Claude Code and the Claude Agent SDK compact automatically near the limit.
82397894c7:
Start from the loop chapter 02 built. The Messages API is stateless. Each request carries the system prompt, the tool definitions and the full conversation, and the model sees only what's in that request.

The harness sends the list and reads stop_reason. If it's "tool_use", the harness executes every requested tool. It appends the assistant turn and one user turn of tool_result blocks, and calls again. When stop_reason is "end_turn", the run is over. That's the whole loop. (Companion: 01_loop_state.py prints the number of messages and the input tokens sent on each turn.)
1e65b69f25:
Look at the loop as a state machine and one thing stands out. There's exactly one piece of state, and it only grows. Each iteration appends two messages. Nothing is ever removed unless your code removes it. There's no hidden server-side session, no cursor, no memory of earlier requests.

If you want the agent to know something on turn 30, it must be in the list sent on turn 30. Either it's been there since turn 1, or a tool put it back.
6b46462698: Cost and latency grow with the list. Each call re-sends everything before it. A 30-turn run pays for turn 1's tokens 30 times. Prompt caching (chapter 15) cuts the price of re-reading an unchanged prefix. It doesn't fix the window limit or the attention cost.
1be16cfe55: Quality degrades with length and noise. As the list fills with large tool outputs, the facts that matter become a smaller share of what the model attends to. They also sit further from the end of the context. Anthropic's guidance calls this context rot: treat the window as a finite budget.
4d25756455: The list must stay valid. Every tool_use block in an assistant turn must be answered by a tool_result with the same id, in the very next user turn. Roles must alternate. Any pruning or summarising must preserve this, or the next request is rejected with HTTP 400.
be55186e28:
A Java analogy fits well. Picture a stateless REST service behind a load balancer. It requires the client to post its entire HTTP session object with every request. You'd never let that session object grow without bound. You'd keep identifiers and a few working values in it, load entities from the database on demand, and write durable changes back. Agent memory design is the same discipline, applied to a session object that the model reads in full, every time.

If you've built sagas, the analogy extends. The message list is the saga log. A checkpointer is the saga store. A sub-agent is a child saga with its own log, whose outcome is reported back as a single event.
6ac3915267: Before choosing remedies, measure the disease. Example 02_token_growth.py runs an agent that checks ten cell sites for critical alarms, one tool call per site. In the verbose version, get_alarms returns all 300 alarm rows for each site, with every field. In the trimmed version, it returns only critical and major rows with five fields, plus a count of suppressed minor alarms. Here are the input tokens the fake client estimated per turn (4 characters per token):
f15cd26826:
Two numbers matter.

The peak is the size of the last request, which must fit in the window. It's about 187k tokens in the verbose run. That would already fail or be truncated on a 200k window with a large system prompt.

The total is the sum over all requests, which is what you pay for (minus caching discounts). Here it's over a million input tokens to answer one question. Each turn re-sends everything before it. So when each call adds a similar amount, total input grows roughly with the square of the number of tool calls. Ten calls of 18k tokens cost about 18k x (1+2+...+10), roughly 1M.

The trimmed tool changed one function and cut the total by a factor of two hundred.
54ccc9f9b2:
Size is half the problem. The other half is attention.

A transformer has no hard rule that drops the middle of a long context. But research on long-context use (for example "Lost in the Middle", Liu et al., 2023) found that models use information at the start and end of a long input more reliably than information buried in the middle. Needle-in-a-haystack style tests show retrieval accuracy varying with position and distractors.

Current Claude models do much better on such tests than 2023 models. The engineering conclusion still stands. Take a fact that appears once, in turn 4, surrounded by 150k tokens of alarm rows. On turn 40, it's less likely to be used correctly than the same fact in a short, recent, clearly labelled block.
7697df48e0:
In production this shows up as three symptoms, and the exam likes to describe them without naming the cause.

  • The agent repeats tool calls it already made, because the earlier result is buried.
  • It confuses identifiers, using the cell or order id from a similar record in a large result.
  • It loses the thread of a multi-step plan, and re-plans from scratch.

Say a question tells you an agent "works on short tasks but degrades on long ones". The answer is a context-management change. It isn't a bigger model, a longer window, a higher turn limit or a sterner prompt.
dccf51b57b:
Sometimes the stem describes behaviour that gets worse as a run gets longer: repeated calls, wrong IDs late in the run, forgotten instructions after many tool calls. Look for the option that reduces or restructures what's in the window. Trim tool outputs, clear used results, keep exact facts in a dedicated block, compact with a progress file, or isolate verbose work in a sub-agent.

The distractors: switch to a larger model, raise the iteration limit, add "remember X" to the system prompt, move to a model with a larger window.
2a7c5319a8: "Memory" covers several mechanisms. They have different lifetimes, different storage, and different paths back into the window. The exam expects you to match the mechanism to the requirement, not to add a vector database to every design. The cleanest way to organise them is by how long the information must survive.
d4362ff415:
Map this onto the outline's words.

  • Short-term memory is the first two rows: the window itself, plus whatever your harness pins into it.
  • Long-term memory is the fourth row, and the third if the task spans days.
  • The memory tool is one specific, Anthropic-defined implementation of long-term memory. It's a client-side tool through which Claude reads and writes files under /memories.

Procedural memory is how you configure the agent. Exam stems usually don't call it "memory". But Claude Code calls CLAUDE.md "memory" (chapter 11), so read stems carefully.
d24ecefc41:
Two design rules follow from the table.

First, working memory is the only memory the model sees. So long-term memory is a retrieval problem: what gets loaded, when, by whom (the model through a tool, or the harness before the call), and how much. A store that's never read back does nothing.

Second, rules that must hold belong in configuration or code, not in learned memory. If a policy must apply on every run, put it in the system prompt. If it must apply deterministically, enforce it in a hook, a graph edge or the tool itself (chapter 02 and chapter 20). Letting the agent "remember" a business rule in a memory file it can edit is a governance problem waiting to happen.
682dc3bef7:
Within one run, the default memory is the history itself. That works until something rewrites the history: compaction, a sliding window, a clearing policy, or a sub-agent hand-off.

The moment you summarise, you're asking a model to decide what was important. Summaries are good at gist and bad at digits. "Investigated Dallas sites; one cell on site 0412 had a transport problem" is a fair summary of forty turns. It has also lost the cell letter, the alarm code and the ticket number.
993c876a84: The fix is to keep exact facts in a separate, structured block. The harness maintains it from structured tool outputs, and no summariser is allowed to rewrite it. When get_alarms returns a CRITICAL row, the harness records target_cell and alarm_code. When get_ticket returns, it records ticket_id. On every call, the harness renders the block into the system prompt (or the first user turn). Example 03_facts_block.py runs both versions.
3deede4f66:
Three details make this robust.

  • The facts come from structured tool output, not from asking the model to extract them. So they're exact.
  • The block is rebuilt every call, so it's always near the start of the context and always current.
  • It's small and labelled, so it costs a few dozen tokens and the model finds it easily.

If you put the block in the system prompt, remember the cost. Changing the system prompt invalidates the prompt-cache prefix from that point (chapter 15). If cache hit rate matters, put the block in a user turn near the end instead, or update it only when a fact changes.
4c3851ba30: In Spring terms, the facts block is a small DTO that you keep in the request scope and serialise into every call. Your service layer populates it from typed responses. It isn't a log, and it isn't a summary. It's the subset of state that downstream steps must not get wrong.
d36463bc48:
Sometimes the important facts come from the conversation, not from a tool. The customer states a callback number, say. Then give the model a small tool such as record_fact(key, value) with an enum of allowed keys, and have the harness store the result in the block.

That keeps the extraction model-driven and the storage deterministic. It's the same split as everywhere else in this guide: the model decides what to try, and code decides what is kept and what is allowed.
dfea7ed16a:
Long-term memory answers a different question. What should the agent know at the start of a new session that it learned in an earlier one?

A customer said on Monday that they want texts, not calls. On Thursday they open a new chat. The Thursday message list starts empty. The Monday list is gone, and it should be, since resending every past conversation would be absurd. Something has to carry "prefers SMS" across.
fc288ffd09:
Anthropic's answer in the Claude API is the memory tool. It's an Anthropic-defined, client-side tool. You declare it in tools with a fixed type. Claude emits tool_use blocks with file commands. Your code executes them against whatever storage you choose, then returns tool_result blocks, as for any tool.

Claude has been trained to use it. It checks its memory directory at the start of a task, records progress and learned facts as it works, and reads them back later.

At the time of writing, the documentation gives the definition as {"type": "memory_20250818", "name": "memory"}. It says the name must be memory and that no beta header is required. It lists the tool as available on Claude 4 and later models. Check the docs before you ship, because tool version strings change.
25b4d3063c:
Execution is yours, so security is yours too. The documentation is explicit. Restrict all operations to /memories. Validate that every path starts with it. Reject ../ traversal. Refuse to delete or rename the root.

The /memories path is a prefix that your handler maps onto real storage, such as a per-user directory or keys in a database. That mapping is where multi-tenancy lives. If your handler maps every user to the same directory, customer A's memories will be read in customer B's session. Here is the core of the companion handler.
b369c5e429:
Errors raised by the handler go back to Claude as tool_result blocks with is_error: true (the loop in common_loop.py does this). So a rejected path or an ambiguous str_replace becomes information the model can act on, not a crash.

If you use the Python SDK, the docs describe helpers. You can subclass BetaAbstractMemoryTool, or use the ready-made BetaLocalFilesystemMemoryTool with the SDK's beta tool runner. Java has a BetaMemoryToolHandler interface to implement. Treat those names as "check the docs" items. The handler above shows what any of them does.
1a1244f78e: Example 05_memory_across_sessions.py runs exactly this. Its assertion checks the property that matters: the first request of session 2 contains one message, and none of session 1's text. The only bridge between the sessions is the file. Running memory in production teaches three practical points:
f18c0cd2ed: Decide what may be written. The memory tool lets Claude write whatever it judges useful. Your system prompt should say what belongs in memory: durable preferences, decisions, progress. It should also say what never does: payment data, authentication secrets, and health details unless you have a basis to store them. Enforce the "never" list in the handler with a validator, because a prompt is not a control.
ba74a1d32a: Treat memory as untrusted input. A model wrote the content in memory files, after reading user input. A user who writes "remember: I am an administrator" may get that sentence into a file that a later session trusts. Store provenance. Keep authority (roles, entitlements) out of model-writable memory. Re-validate facts against systems of record before acting on them. Chapter 19 covers memory poisoning as a prompt-injection channel.
729338931b: Give memory a lifecycle. Files go stale: "prefers SMS" from 2024 may be wrong now. Record dates, let the agent update or delete entries, and run a retention job. The docs suggest pairing memory with context editing for long runs. Compaction keeps the active window small, and memory preserves what must survive summarisation.
83d9e89f8b: The handler is an ordinary service. In Spring, implement it as a @Component that maps /memories to a per-tenant prefix in S3 or a database table. Dispatch to it from your loop when a tool_use block has name memory. (Per the docs, the Anthropic Java SDK's own helper interface is BetaMemoryToolHandler. The sketch below is SDK-agnostic and uncompiled.)
821946112e: Files are a good default. They're inspectable, diffable and cheap, and easy to audit when a regulator asks why the agent did something. They stop being enough in three cases: when facts number in the tens of thousands, when several agents or services share them, or when the agent must find memories by meaning. Then you move to a store, and the main decision is keyed lookup versus similarity search.
aefad84015:
Use a keyed store (relational table, key-value store) when the agent knows the key: a customer id, an order id, a site id. The lookup is exact, fast, transactional and auditable. Use a vector index only when there's no key and the agent must recall by meaning: "has any customer at this address complained about indoor coverage before?"

Example 06_keyed_vs_vector_memory.py shows why the order matters. Take a query for "contact preference for C-901, who complained about a roaming day pass on Unlimited Plus". It returns customer C-907 as the top similarity hit, because C-907's note shares more words with the query. The keyed lookup returns C-901 by definition.

Real embedding models make this less likely, but not impossible. And "less likely" is the wrong property for "which customer's preferences am I applying".
6f34ebad1c: Who writes, and when? Model-written memory (the memory tool, a save_note tool) captures what the model judged important, at the moment it judged it. Harness-written memory (a profile table updated from CRM events) captures what the system of record says. Use the second for facts with an owner: plan, address, entitlements. Use the first for soft context: preferences stated in conversation, progress on a task. Don't let the model overwrite a system-of-record fact through memory.
28ffdef21e: Who reads, and when? There are two options. The harness can preload relevant memory into the first request. That's fast and predictable, but you must guess what's relevant. Or the model can retrieve on demand through a tool. That's flexible, but it costs a turn, and the model may not think to look. A common split is to preload a short profile keyed by customer id and let the model search the long tail. The memory tool's documented behaviour, checking /memories at the start of a task, is model-driven retrieval with a strong default.
83cadd4d71:
Claude Code has its own memory layer: CLAUDE.md files at user, project and directory level. That's procedural memory loaded at session start (chapter 11 covers the hierarchy and the /memory command).

LangGraph separates thread-scoped state (checkpointer) from cross-thread memory (a "store" interface keyed by namespace). Strands has session managers that persist agent state. PydanticAI leaves persistence to you, and gives you the message history to save. The vocabulary differs, but every one of them is a row in the table above.
5473712389:
A checkpoint is the agent's state written to durable storage after each step, keyed by a thread or session id. It solves two problems that long-term memory doesn't.

The first is crash recovery. A forty-minute investigation shouldn't restart from zero because a pod was rescheduled.

The second is pausing. A refund over the agent's limit should wait, possibly for hours, for a supervisor. Then it should continue exactly where it stopped, in a different process.
6db2c5e2ff:
The mechanics are simple, and the details are where bugs live. Example 15_checkpoint_resume.py writes the message list to a JSON file twice per turn: once after appending the assistant turn, and once after appending the tool results.

Then it simulates a crash in the gap between the two. The model has asked for get_tracking, and the assistant turn is saved, but the tool never ran. On restart, the saved list ends with an unanswered tool_use, which the API would reject. The resume path must repair it.
cf1d8e1d4d:
Which repair to choose depends on the tool. Re-executing is correct for reads, and for writes protected by an idempotency key. It's the same key the payments world uses: the refund id is derived from the conversation and the order, so a second issue_refund with the same key is a no-op.

Dropping the turn is the safe default when you can't prove idempotency, because the model will simply ask again. What you must never do is assume the tool ran. A refund that was never issued but reported as issued is the most expensive bug in this chapter.
723f79b4ad:
Frameworks package this.

  • LangGraph's checkpointer saves state after every node ("super-step") under config={"configurable": {"thread_id": ...}}. It reloads it on the next invoke with the same thread id. Its interrupt() function pauses a node, and Command(resume=value) continues it (section 16).
  • The Claude Agent SDK persists sessions, so you can resume or fork them by session id (chapter 02).
  • Strands has session managers that persist agent state to files or S3 (check the docs for current class names).

For a Spring team, the nearest equivalent is Spring State Machine with a persisted StateMachineContext. Or use a workflow engine such as Temporal, whose event history and deterministic replay are a more industrial version of the same idea.
69e4ea88b9: Chapter 16 treats context engineering as a whole discipline. Here the question is narrower. What does an agent harness do, turn by turn, to keep the list small, valid and focused? There are six techniques. Order matters, because the early ones are cheaper and lose less information than the later ones. Reach for them from the top.
944eaa7c66: Do not load it (just-in-time retrieval). Keep identifiers in context (file paths, ticket ids, URLs, row keys), and let the agent fetch content with a tool when it needs it. Claude Code works this way. It uses Glob and Grep to locate, and Read for the few files that matter, instead of pasting a repository into the prompt.
3301e53ffa: Trim at the tool. A tool that returns 300 rows when the agent needs one is a tool-design bug. Filter, project fields, paginate, and summarise logs inside the tool. Say in the result what was suppressed ("297 minor alarms suppressed"). Example 02 showed a factor of 200.
5dfeae34cd: Compact. When the history is still too long, summarise older turns into a block and continue from it. It's lossy, so protect exact facts with a facts block (section 06) or memory. Server-side compaction, the Agent SDK and Claude Code all offer it (section 12).
d73f71c0c7: Isolate in a sub-agent. Some sub-tasks generate a lot of intermediate context: reading three long logs, searching sixty files. Run them in a sub-agent whose window is discarded. Only a short result returns (section 14).
c0f1e003df: A bigger context window is conspicuously absent from the ladder. It's sometimes the right answer, for a single large document that must be read whole. But for an agent accumulating tool output, it delays the failure, raises cost per turn, and leaves the attention problem in place. The exam treats "use the model with the larger window" as a distractor whenever the stem describes accumulation.
6a17c086bb: The obvious way to shrink history is to delete old tool results. It's also the way to break the request. The API checks that every tool_use id in an assistant turn has a tool_result in the next user turn. Delete the result, and the next call fails with a 400 naming the orphaned id. Example 07_clear_tool_results.py shows both versions against the fake client, which applies the same check.
0910d2e833:
Three design choices are visible in the fixed version, and in the API feature it mirrors.

  • Oldest first, keep the last N. Recent results are the ones the model is most likely still reasoning about.
  • Placeholder text that tells the model what happened. If it needs the data again, it can call the tool again. That's cheap compared with carrying the payload for thirty turns.
  • An exclusion list. Some results must never be cleared, typically memory-tool reads or a policy document the agent must keep consulting.
195adfd003:
The Claude API can apply the same policy server-side, so you don't have to rewrite history yourself. At the time of writing, it's a beta feature. You enable it with the context-management-2025-06-27 beta and a context_management request field.

The documented tool-clearing strategy is clear_tool_uses_20250919, with these parameters:

  • trigger: default 100,000 input tokens; can be expressed in input tokens or tool uses;
  • keep: default the 3 most recent tool uses;
  • clear_at_least: a minimum number of tokens to clear, so that clearing is worth invalidating the cache;
  • exclude_tools;
  • clear_tool_inputs: default false; also clears the call parameters.

A separate clear_thinking_20251015 strategy manages old thinking blocks. Check the docs before shipping, because beta names change.
58efc525a8:
Two operational consequences.

First, server-side clearing happens on the server's copy of the prompt. But your stored history still has the full payloads. So your logs stay complete, and your next request still sends them (the server clears again). That's good for audit, and it costs bandwidth, not tokens.

Second, clearing changes the prompt prefix from the first cleared block onward. That invalidates the prompt cache from that point. clear_at_least exists so that you only pay that cost when the saving is large. Example 09_server_context_management.py prints the request body and simulates the response's applied_edits.
2bcdd03884:
Clearing removes payloads, but it leaves every turn in place. On a long enough run, even the skeleton is too long: hundreds of turns of reasoning and placeholders. Compaction replaces the older part of the history with a summary, and continues from it.

Claude Code does this automatically near the context limit, and exposes /compact (with optional instructions about what to keep). The Claude Agent SDK compacts automatically. And the API offers server-side compaction.
035cced7b0:
Writing your own compaction is a good way to understand the constraints, and example 08_compaction.py does it. The policy tries the cheap step first (clear used results). It compacts only if the history is still over budget.

Compaction must respect three invariants:

  • the summary must not split a tool_use from its tool_result;
  • the new list must start with a user turn and keep roles alternating;
  • exact facts must survive, which the summary alone can't guarantee.
c424294e2c:
At the time of writing, the API's threshold compaction is a context-management edit of type compact_20260112, behind the compact-2026-01-12 beta. Its documented parameters are:

  • trigger: input tokens, default 150,000, minimum 50,000;
  • pause_after_compaction: default false;
  • instructions: a custom summarisation prompt that replaces the default entirely.

When it fires, the response contains a compaction content block holding the summary. You append the assistant turn as usual, and the API drops everything before that block on later requests. With pause_after_compaction, the response returns with stop_reason: "compaction". Your code can then inspect or add to the summary before continuing. The docs also describe on-demand compaction under a separate beta.

All of this is new and in beta. Check the docs for current names. And treat "compaction" as one more stop reason your loop must handle explicitly, not as a finish.
5878f653a9:
Compaction is lossy by design. That's why the documentation recommends pairing it with memory. Compaction keeps the active context small, and memory (or your facts block) preserves the information that must survive summarisation.

If you remember one sentence from this section, make it this one. A summary is a model's opinion of what mattered; a facts block or a memory file is a record.
b727995969:
Some tasks won't fit in any window: migrating nine microservices from Spring Boot 2.7 to 3.3, reconciling a quarter of roaming records, working through a backlog of 200 tickets. Compaction alone degrades over many cycles, because each summary is a summary of a summary.

The pattern that holds up is structured note-taking. The agent maintains a progress file (or a memory-tool file) outside the window. Each new window starts from the task brief plus that file, not from the old conversation.
970e8e3d4d:
Anthropic's guidance on long-running agents describes this pattern: a progress log plus a feature or task list, committed as the agent works. Claude Code users apply it with a PROGRESS.md or a TODO list.

Example 16_progress_notes.py runs it. There are nine services and three windows of three services each. Every window starts with a single message containing the brief and a JSON progress object. The assertions check that no service was migrated twice, and none was skipped.
acf5cb56f6:
Make the notes structured (JSON, or Markdown with fixed headings), so the harness can validate them. No item should be in both done and pending, and every blocked item needs a reason.

Record decisions with reasons ("porting: kept javax.xml.bind via a Jakarta shim; revisit in Q1"). Decisions are what a fresh window is most likely to re-litigate.

And make the source of truth checkable where you can. If the task is a code migration, "done" should mean "the build passed and the commit exists". The next window can verify that with git, rather than just believe it.
1882632987:
Chapter 01 treats sub-agents as an architecture choice (orchestrator-workers, hierarchies). As a pattern in 1.3, the point is narrower and mechanical: a sub-agent is a function call with its own context window.

The lead writes a brief. The sub-agent runs its own loop, with its own tools, for as many turns as it needs, and returns a short result. Its window, with all its intermediate tool output, is then discarded. The lead's window grows only by the size of the brief plus the result.
213e80ca14:
Example 10_subagent_isolation.py measures it. An incident lead must find the cause of VoLTE drops, and the evidence is in three eNodeB logs.

When the lead reads the logs itself, its peak input is about 6,850 (fake) tokens. All of that stays in its window for every later turn. When it delegates to a log-analyst sub-agent through one tool call, its peak is about 208 tokens. The sub-agent paid for the logs in its own window, using a cheaper model, and returned three fields.
577d3b963b:
Isolation cuts both ways, and that's the exam point. The sub-agent inherits nothing from the lead's conversation. In the Claude Agent SDK, the Task tool starts a sub-agent with its own fresh context. The only channel from parent to child is the prompt string the parent writes (chapter 02).

A brief such as "check the logs for the issue we discussed" gives the sub-agent nothing: no site, no time window, no symptom, no output format. Example 11_subagent_context_passing.py checks this mechanically.
1e66c0134f:
A good brief has four parts, the same parts as a good API contract:

  • the goal: what question to answer, not a procedure;
  • the known facts, so the sub-agent doesn't redo the lead's work;
  • the constraints: tools, read-only, budget;
  • the output contract: fields, limits, format.

The output contract is the part teams forget. It's also the part that decides whether isolation saves anything. A sub-agent told only "summarise the logs" may return 3,000 tokens of log excerpts.
2bae87cd9b: Here is the same pattern with the Claude Agent SDK, which you met in chapter 02. The sub-agent is declared with an AgentDefinition (description, prompt, tools, model). The lead must have Task in its allowed tools to delegate. The sub-agent's tools are read-only.
1a05921570:
The costs are real. Multi-agent runs use more tokens in total than a single agent doing the same work, because each sub-agent pays for its own system prompt, tools and reading. Sequential delegations add latency. And the hand-off is lossy: if the result contract omits a field the lead needed, the lead must delegate again or guess.

Sub-agents are worth it when the sub-task is:

  • separable: it can be specified in a brief;
  • verbose: it generates far more context than its conclusion;
  • ideally parallel: several sub-agents can run at once.

For a three-call lookup, a sub-agent is overhead.
f8ed279fad:
The objective names three third-party frameworks: LangGraph, Strands Agents and PydanticAI. None of them changes what Claude can do. On every step, each one still builds a Messages API request (or the equivalent on Bedrock or Vertex), reads the stop reason, runs tools and appends results.

What they change is who owns the control flow, how state is represented, and what is guaranteed. Read each of the next three sections as an answer to four questions. Where is the loop? Where is the state? How is context managed? And where would I put a guardrail that must always hold?
3f8c5e1c24:
A word about the code in the next three sections. Each section shows the framework's code the way its documentation presents it: imports, decorators, constructor arguments as of late 2026. Framework APIs move quickly, so verify against the current docs.

The companion folder runs the same programs offline. stubs/mini_langgraph.py, stubs/mini_strands.py and stubs/mini_pydanticai.py are small stand-ins that copy the public shape of each library over the fake client. You can trace exactly what each framework does to the message list without installing anything. They're teaching stubs, not the libraries.
982c2f4f29:
LangGraph models an application as a graph.

  • State is a typed dictionary (a TypedDict or Pydantic model).
  • Nodes are functions that take the state and return a partial update.
  • Reducers, attached to state keys with Annotated, say how updates merge. The built-in add_messages reducer appends new messages (and replaces messages with a matching id) instead of overwriting the list.
  • Edges decide what runs next. Conditional edges call a routing function on the state.

You compile the graph, optionally with a checkpointer that saves state after every step under a thread_id.
82fac478f4:
Because you draw the edges, you own the control flow. That's the reason to choose LangGraph. An approval node can sit between "plan the port resubmission" and "resubmit the port", and the model can't route around it. Routing is your Python function, not the model's choice.

The checkpointer gives you resume after a crash, and inspection of every intermediate state ("time travel"). It also gives you human-in-the-loop. Inside a node, interrupt(payload) pauses the graph and returns the payload to the caller. Later, graph.invoke(Command(resume=value), config) with the same thread_id re-runs that node, and this time interrupt() returns value. Interrupts require a checkpointer.

If you know Spring State Machine or a BPMN engine, LangGraph is that idea with a model inside some states.
c2c104f13b: Run 12_langgraph_port_agent.py and look at its printed node trace: agent -> tools -> agent -> approval -> approval -> tools -> agent. Why does the approval node appear twice? As the LangGraph docs warn, a resumed node restarts from the beginning, so any code before interrupt() runs again. Keep side effects after the interrupt, or make them idempotent. And keep the order of multiple interrupt() calls in a node stable.
063d06bb37:
In LangGraph, context management is your job, done in state. Common approaches:

  • a node that trims or summarises messages before the agent node (LangChain ships message-trimming helpers; check the docs);
  • structured facts kept as separate state keys (like order_id above), so they never depend on the message history;
  • LangGraph's cross-thread store for long-term memory, keyed by namespace (for example per customer).

The trade-off of the whole framework is explicitness. You write more code, and you must model the flow up front. For tasks whose steps you can't predict, a fixed graph becomes a liability. You end up with a single agent node looping on itself, which is what the next two frameworks give you by default.
51df2eb65b:
Strands Agents, open-sourced by AWS in 2025, takes the opposite position. You give an Agent a model, a system prompt and a list of tools, and call agent("..."). The model runs the loop. Tools are Python functions decorated with @tool. The docstring becomes the description, and the type hints become the input schema.

The default model provider is Amazon Bedrock, and there are providers for the Anthropic API and others. It supports MCP tools, multi-agent patterns (agents as tools, swarms, graphs), hooks on lifecycle events, and session persistence. Choose it when you want the least orchestration code and your platform standard is AWS.
b2b8c23c7e:
Context management in Strands is a pluggable conversation manager on the agent. The documentation lists three in Python, imported from strands.agent.conversation_manager:

  • SlidingWindowConversationManager: the default. It keeps the most recent messages (window_size default 20) and can truncate oversized tool results.
  • SummarizingConversationManager: summarises older messages. Parameters include summary_ratio and preserve_recent_messages, and an optional separate summarisation agent or prompt.
  • NullConversationManager: no management.

The Strands docs note that the sliding window trims carefully, so tool-use and tool-result pairs aren't split. That's the same invariant as section 11.
7261ed68f9: The sliding window is easy to reason about, and it has an obvious failure mode, which example 13 demonstrates. A reservation is made, and the user asks a follow-up. A window of six messages drops the first exchange, and the reservation id R-55102 is no longer anywhere in the context. If a later step needs that id, it's gone. The fix is the same as in section 06. Keep facts the agent must not lose in agent state or memory, not only in the conversation.
80e3809318:
Notice the system prompt: "Always check inventory first." That's a request to the model, not a control. In example 13, the scripted model skips the check on its first attempt. A guard denies the call with an error result. The model then checks inventory and retries.

In real Strands, deterministic guards go in hooks or in the tool itself. A hook here is a hook provider registered on the agent that can inspect or cancel tool calls (check the docs for the current event names). In the tool, reserve_device checks stock before reserving.

It's the same lesson as hooks in chapter 02, and the exam asks it whatever the framework. When the requirement says "always", "never" or "guarantee", the answer is code.
20947d624f:
PydanticAI, from the Pydantic team, brings type safety to agents. An Agent declares two types.

  • A dependency type: database handles, the authenticated customer, HTTP clients. It's passed in at run time and injected into tools through a RunContext[Deps] first parameter.
  • An output type: a Pydantic model, or another type, that the final answer must validate against.

When validation fails, the framework sends the validation errors back to the model and lets it try again, up to a retry limit. A tool can also raise ModelRetry("...") to tell the model its arguments were wrong and ask it to retry. Model strings look like "anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5".
172c5d6a80:
For a Spring developer the mapping is direct. deps_type is constructor injection. RunContext is the injected context. The output model is a DTO with Bean Validation annotations. And the retry on validation failure is what you'd otherwise hand-write in a controller advice.

The design consequence: tools never reach for globals, and never trust the model for identity. The customer id comes from ctx.deps, set by your authenticated request handler. It doesn't come from a tool argument the model filled in.
cc06dba450: The offline version scripts a model that makes two mistakes. It prints what goes back to the model:
dc36bde3b2:
The first error came from ModelRetry in the tool. The second came from Pydantic rejecting "international" as a category and -40 as an amount. Both became tool_result blocks with is_error, and the model corrected itself.

With tool-capable models, PydanticAI implements structured output by default through a final-result tool whose schema is the output model. (It also supports other output modes; check the docs.) That's why the stub does the same.
d8ba802d69:
Two limits to keep in mind.

Validation guarantees shape, not truth. The model can still return "roaming" for a dispute that is really a plan change. Typed output removes parsing errors, not judgment errors. Chapter 18 covers semantic checks, and chapter 05 the API's own structured outputs.

And PydanticAI doesn't manage context or persistence for you. result.all_messages() gives you the history, and you decide what to store, trim and pass back as message_history. That's a feature for teams that want control. For long-running agents it's a gap, unless you add the techniques from sections 10 to 13.
b9bd4432f7:
The exam's bias, and Anthropic's published advice, is to start with the simplest thing that works. That means direct API calls and a loop you can read, with framework layers added only when they solve a stated need. Frameworks help you start quickly. But they add abstraction that can hide the exact prompts and responses, and that makes debugging harder.

Whatever you choose, make sure you can log the exact request and response sent to the model on every step. With that bias in mind, here is how the requirement maps to the choice.
2b6fb4a14d:
A Spring team has options that map onto the same three shapes. So the concepts transfer, even though the exam's named frameworks are Python-first.

  • Spring AI provides a ChatClient with tool calling, and a ChatMemory abstraction with message-window memory and pluggable repositories (JDBC, Cassandra, and others), applied through advisors. That's the Strands-like, model-driven shape with a sliding window.
  • LangGraph4j is a community Java port of LangGraph's state graph and checkpoint ideas.
  • Spring State Machine or Temporal give you the explicit-graph-with-durable-state shape, and they're battle-tested for long-running processes. You call the model from inside states or activities.
  • For the PydanticAI shape, Bean Validation on a record that the model fills through a forced tool call, plus a retry loop, is a few dozen lines.

Class and package names in Spring AI have changed across releases. Check the docs for the version you use.
ced6c645a0: Work through each scenario before reading the reasoning. The wrong options are usually plausible: a bigger model, a prompt instruction, or a framework that sounds right for the wrong requirement.
5aad8947d5:
The symptoms (repeats, wrong ids, only on long runs) point to context accumulation. The facts are present but buried. C reduces what enters the window, moves verbose work to a disposable window, and pins exact facts deterministically.

A may help slightly, but it leaves the cause and costs more. B is a probabilistic request that moves nothing. D lets the agent run longer in the same degraded state.
05eff4b328:
The requirement is durable, per-customer facts. B is the purpose-built mechanism, with tenancy and safety in the handler and a write policy in the prompt.

A fills the window with stale bulk and grows without bound. C is slow and expensive, and it can't be updated or deleted per customer. D is fuzzy retrieval for keyed facts, and the first message may not be about preferences at all.
bb7be05288:
The API requires every tool_use to be answered in the next user turn. B keeps the structure and drops the bulk. That's exactly what clear_tool_uses_20250919 does server-side.

A can work mechanically, but it deletes the model's own reasoning record and risks breaking alternation. It's a worse version of B. C changes the agent's capabilities to hide a bug. D limits output, not input history.
2fff3013fc:
The requirements (pause for hours, survive restarts, explicit and auditable flow) map to a checkpointed graph with an interrupt.

A relies on a prompt for a must-hold rule. C validates the shape of output, but the model fills the field itself, so it isn't an approval. D doesn't survive restarts, and it ties up resources. (A hook-based deny plus session resume in the Agent SDK would also work. It isn't offered here.)
1a073bf05f:
Sub-agents inherit nothing; the brief is their only context. B fixes the hand-off and keeps isolation.

A defeats the purpose of isolation and copies irrelevant bulk. C doesn't supply the missing facts. D may be correct for small tasks, but the stem's problem is the brief, not the decision to delegate.
4939f5f372: Run 02_token_growth.py. Change the verbose tool to return 100 rows instead of 300, and predict the new total before rerunning. Was your estimate within 10%? Explain the quadratic term in one sentence.
4bde00b80e: In 13_strands_store_agent.py, move the reservation id into a facts block that the agent object keeps. The follow-up question should still see it after the sliding window trims.
4ecb010818: Optional, with an API key: replace the fake client in 05_memory_across_sessions.py with anthropic.Anthropic(), and keep the handler. Watch what the real model writes to /memories in session 1.
577e0e12be: Done when: you can explain, for each technique on the ladder in section 10, what it costs and what it loses. Every 400 you caused in steps 3 and 4 makes sense from the pairing rule. And you can name the deciding requirement for LangGraph, Strands and PydanticAI without looking.
